steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm head of household in Chicago IL. W-2 from TechStart Inc: $91,000. Additional income: $22,100 (web design, 2 clients), $1,450 from Discover Bank savings, $320 from Charles Schwab. Home office: 140 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,600/month for 690 sq ft. Deductions: $4,400 student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2020); $1,350 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) with receipt; $890 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — useful detail. Below I’ll cover what looks deductible, how to treat the home office, whether you’ll likely itemize or take the standard deduction, the forms you’ll need, and a few actions/questions so I can run more exact numbers if you want.

Short answer summary
- Report your W-2 wages, self‑employment (web design) income, and interest income on your 1040.
- Your web‑design income is reported on Schedule C; you can deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses (including a home‑office deduction) there. You’ll also file Schedule SE to compute self‑employment tax.
- Your bank interest (Discover + Schwab = $1,770) must be reported; because combined interest > $1,500 you’ll also file Schedule B.
- The $1,350 donation is deductible only if you itemize. Based on the items you listed, the standard deduction for Head of Household will almost certainly be larger than your itemized total — so you’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction.
- The student‑loan interest deduction is an above‑the‑line adjustment (up to $2,500), but it phases out based on MAGI. With $91K wages + $22.1K self‑employment, you will very likely be above the phaseout and therefore not eligible for that deduction unless you reduce MAGI (see note below).
- Keep receipts and records (donation receipt, Form 1098‑E for student loans, business receipts, rent/utility records for home office).

What you can deduct (based on what you gave)
- Self‑employment/business expenses (Schedule C): ordinary business costs related to your web design clients. If the $890 is business-related (hosting, software, travel, supplies), it’s deductible on Schedule C. If the $890 is unreimbursed expenses from an employer (W‑2 job), post‑2017 law generally disallows those deductions.
- Home office: deductible if you use 140 sq ft exclusively and regularly as your principal place of business. You have two methods:
  - Actual (proportionate) method — your business percentage = 140 / 690 ≈ 20.3%. You can deduct 20.3% of allocable housing expenses (rent $1,600/mo = $19,200/yr → ≈ $3,898 attributable to the office) plus a share of utilities and other allowable home expenses. You compute this and report via Form 8829 (business use of home) and transfer the deduction to Schedule C.
  - Simplified method — $5 per sq ft × 140 sq ft = $700 (max 300 sq ft). No Form 8829 needed; you report the simplified deduction on Schedule C.
  - In your case the actual method (just counting rent alone) looks to give a bigger deduction (~$3,900) than the simplified $700 — but only if you have and want to allocate other home expenses correctly and meet the exclusive/principal place tests.
- Self‑employment tax deduction: you can deduct half of your self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.
- Charitable contributions: $1,350 to a qualified charity is deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A).
- Student loan interest: up to $2,500 allowed as an adjustment on Schedule 1, but phases out based on MAGI. With the income figures you gave, you’re very likely above the phaseout (see calculations below).

What you cannot deduct (from your list)
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for your W‑2 job (suspended for most taxpayers).
- If the $890 is unrelated to the business (e.g., personal), it’s not deductible on Schedule C.

Quick illustrative numbers (estimates showing effect of home‑office choice)
Assumptions: $22,100 self‑employment gross receipts; $890 business expenses (if they are business expenses). Interest income total = $1,770.

- If you use the actual home‑office allocation (rent only):
  - Home‑office rent portion ≈ $3,898
  - Total business expenses = $3,898 + $890 = $4,788
  - Net self‑employment profit ≈ $22,100 − $4,788 = $17,312
  - Self‑employment tax ≈ $2,450; half of that (~$1,225) is an adjustment to income.
- If you use the simplified method:
  - Home‑office deduction = $700
  - Total business expenses = $700 + $890 = $1,590
  - Net profit ≈ $22,100 − $1,590 = $20,510
  - Self‑employment tax ≈ $2,900; half (~$1,450) adjustment to income.

Either way you report the business on Schedule C and SE; the actual method reduces net profit and SE tax more than the simplified method in this scenario.

Student‑loan interest (the important phaseout)
- The student‑loan interest deduction phases out by MAGI. For single/head‑of‑household filers in recent years, the phaseout started around ~$75k and ended around ~$90k (these amounts are indexed annually). With roughly $91k W‑2 + ~$22k business (even after deductions) + interest, your MAGI is well above the typical phaseout ceiling, so you likely cannot claim the student‑loan interest deduction. If you want, I can compute exact MAGI and whether any of the $4,400 qualifies given 2024 thresholds.

Standard deduction vs itemize
- You listed $1,350 charitable giving as your main itemized deduction. Unless you have significant state/local taxes, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, or other itemizable deductions you did not list, the Head‑of‑Household standard deduction will be far larger than $1,350 — so take the standard deduction.
- Bottom line: almost certainly take the standard deduction instead of itemizing based on the info provided.

Forms you’ll need (federal)
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report web‑design income and business expenses, including the home‑office deduction (line 30).
- Schedule SE — compute self‑employment tax.
- Schedule 1 — for adjustments (e.g., half of SE tax, student‑loan interest if allowed), and to report business income adjustment flow.
- Schedule B — for interest and ordinary dividends (required because your interest > $1,500).
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the actual method for the home office; not needed for the simplified method.
- Schedule A — only if you choose to itemize (unlikely based on current numbers).
- Form 1099‑NEC / 1099‑K — you should include any 1099s received for client payments; even if you received no 1099, you still report all self‑employment income.
- Form 1098‑E — your student loan servicer should provide this; used to substantiate the interest paid.
- Illinois state return (IL‑1040) — file state taxes for Illinois.

Other practical items and recommendations
- Keep the donation receipt for Northwest Harvest; keep receipts for all business expenses and proof of exclusive use for your home office (floor plan, photos, lease/rent statements, utility bills).
- If you haven’t been making estimated tax payments for the self‑employment income quarter‑by‑quarter, you may owe estimated taxes and/or penalties; consider making estimated payments (Form 1040‑ES) or increasing withholding on your W‑2 job to cover tax + SE tax.
- Consider whether pre‑tax retirement contributions (traditional IRA, SEP IRA, or Solo 401(k)) might make sense — they can reduce taxable income and self‑employment tax (depending on plan) and could potentially help with MAGI‑based phaseouts (like the student loan interest phaseout) — consult a tax advisor for retirement contribution strategy.
- If any of the $890 expense is actually unreimbursed expenses from your employer (not related to your self‑employment), it is generally nondeductible.

Questions I need to finalize exact numbers
1. Is the $890 definitely business expenses for your web‑design activity (hosting, software, travel, supplies)? Or are they unreimbursed employee expenses for your W‑2 job?
2. Do you have any mortgage interest, property tax, large state taxes paid, or other itemizable deductions not listed?
3. Do you have other home expenses (utilities, renters’ insurance, repairs) you want to allocate to the actual home‑office method?
4. Did you receive any 1099‑NEC or 1099‑K for the web‑design income? Do you have Form 1098‑E from Cornerstone for student loan interest?
5. Want me to run the exact AGI/taxable income calculations using the actual vs simplified home‑office methods (and estimate tax owed)?

I can compute a detailed estimate of AGI, taxable income, self‑employment tax, and whether the student‑loan interest deduction survives if you want — just tell me answers to the questions above (especially #1 and #3). Also note: I’m giving general guidance; for definitive, situation‑specific tax planning, consult a CPA or tax preparer.
